posts.after: The lawsuit clock starts the day you are hurt: Georgia allows two years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina three (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). A Georgia plaintiff found 50% or more at fault recovers nothing (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), while South Carolina permits recovery at 50% or less, reduced by that share (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Claims against government move faster. Georgia requires ante litem notice within six months for a city (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5) and twelve months for a county or the State (O.C.G.A. §§ 36-11-1, 50-21-26). South Carolina's Tort Claims Act allows two years to sue, or three after a verified claim (S.C. Code §§ 15-78-110, 15-78-80). Roden Law takes injury cases on contingency, with free consultations at its offices in both states.

An e-bike rider injured by someone else's negligence must file within two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) or three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). These claims often have two targets: the driver who caused the collision, and the maker or seller of a battery, motor or brake that failed. Keep the bike, charger and battery as they are, because the hardware is the evidence. Expect the other side to say you were riding too fast. That argument defeats a Georgia claim only at 50% fault or more (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), and a South Carolina claim only above 50% (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Roden Law accepts e-bike cases on contingency and gives a free first consultation at its offices in both states.

Golf cart injury claims carry the ordinary injury deadlines: two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). What sets them apart is the number of possible defendants. A crash in a resort, gated community or beach town can involve the driver, the rental outfit, the association or course that maintains the paths, and the manufacturer when brakes or steering fail. Most carts have no doors, so passengers are thrown easily. Georgia denies recovery at 50% responsibility (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), and South Carolina denies it above 50% (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Roden Law handles golf cart claims on contingency, and the initial consultation at its offices in Georgia and South Carolina costs nothing.

For ATV and side-by-side injuries, Georgia's filing period is two years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina's is three (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Most of these crashes happen off the road, on farms, trails or rental courses, so liability usually turns on the landowner, the tour operator, the adult who let a child ride, or a rollover, throttle or steering defect. Preserve the machine and any waiver you signed. If the defense says you rode recklessly, your recovery is reduced by your share and lost once it reaches 50% in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) or passes 50% in South Carolina (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Roden Law pursues off-road injury cases for a contingency fee and offers a free consultation at its offices in Georgia and South Carolina.

A scooter rider's deadline depends on who is responsible. Against a private driver or rental company, suit is due within two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). If a pothole caused the fall, a Georgia city must receive ante litem notice within six months (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5), and a county within twelve (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1). A South Carolina government entity must be sued within two years, or three if a verified claim was filed first (S.C. Code §§ 15-78-110, 15-78-80). Rider fault bars recovery at 50% in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) or above 50% in South Carolina (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Roden Law works these claims for a contingency fee, with free consultations at its Georgia and South Carolina offices.

A cyclist struck by a car in Georgia has two years to sue (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33); in South Carolina the period is three years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). The passing rules differ. Georgia drivers must leave at least three feet when overtaking a bicycle (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-56). South Carolina names no distance and requires only a safe operating distance (S.C. Code § 56-5-3435). Drivers' insurers often claim the cyclist swerved. Georgia lets you recover while your share is under 50% (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33); South Carolina, while it is no more than 50% (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Roden Law's bicycle accident lawyers charge only a contingency fee and meet new clients free of charge at offices in Georgia and South Carolina.

If a vehicle hit you on foot, you have two years to file suit in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Where signals are absent or not working, South Carolina drivers must yield to a pedestrian in a marked or unmarked crosswalk (S.C. Code § 56-5-3130). In Georgia, a person crossing outside a crosswalk must yield to vehicles, so right of way depends on where you crossed (O.C.G.A. § 40-6-92). Crossing mid-block still leaves room to recover: Georgia bars only a pedestrian 50% or more at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), and South Carolina only one above 50% (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Roden Law takes pedestrian cases on contingency and consults free at its offices in both states.

Anyone hurt by a dangerous condition on someone else's property has two years to sue in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Inadequate security, pool hazards and falling merchandise all qualify, and each rests on proof of what the owner knew and when. Ownership can change the damages. In South Carolina, a claim against a charitable organization for its employee's negligence is limited to actual damages within the Tort Claims Act caps (S.C. Code § 33-56-180). A Georgia claim fails at 50% visitor fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33); a South Carolina claim fails above 50% (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Roden Law takes property-injury cases on contingency, with a free consultation at any of its offices in both states.

Families who suspect nursing home abuse or neglect should act early, because harm can go unnoticed for months. The general injury deadline is two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Where the harm arises from medical care, South Carolina counts a nursing home as a health care institution, so its malpractice cap on non-economic damages can apply (S.C. Code § 15-32-220). A nonprofit facility's liability for its employees may also be limited (S.C. Code § 33-56-180). Blaming the resident works only at 50% fault in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) or above 50% in South Carolina (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Roden Law brings these cases for a contingency fee, and families consult free at its Georgia and South Carolina offices.

A construction injury usually opens two claims with separate clocks. The benefits claim is generally due within one year of the injury in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82) and two years of the accident in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 42-15-40). A South Carolina contractor that subcontracted the work can be the statutory employer who owes those benefits (S.C. Code § 42-1-410). A suit against an outside party, such as a scaffold maker, must be filed within two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Your fault bars it at 50% in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) or above 50% in South Carolina (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Roden Law pursues both on contingency, with free consultations at offices in both states.

A burn injury caused by another party's negligence must be taken to court within two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) or three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Establishing what started the fire comes first: a faulty appliance or battery, a gas leak, missing smoke detectors or an industrial failure each points to a different defendant. Preserve the scene, the device and any wiring before cleanup. Severe burns also mean documenting years of grafts, scar care and lost work. Georgia allows compensation below 50% fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) and South Carolina at 50% or less (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.), each reduced by your share. Roden Law represents burn survivors on contingency, and a consultation at its offices in either state is free.

When state law governs a boating injury, Georgia allows two years to file (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina three (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Where on the water the accident happened can affect which rules apply, so record the location, the vessels and their registration numbers at once. Responsible parties often include the operator, the owner who lent the boat, a rental or charter company, a marina, or the maker of failed equipment. Impaired operation, excessive wake and no lookout are common grounds. Under state law, Georgia allows no recovery at 50% or greater fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), and South Carolina none above 50% (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Roden Law takes boating cases for a contingency fee and offers a free consultation at its Georgia and South Carolina offices.

If a defective product injured you, Georgia gives you two years from the injury to sue (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33), and South Carolina gives you three (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). The investigation covers the whole chain of distribution, from the designer and component supplier to the manufacturer, distributor and retailer. The product is the key evidence, so keep it unrepaired with its packaging, manual and receipt, and never return it to the seller. Manufacturers commonly argue misuse or alteration. On a negligence claim, if the jury assigns you part of the blame, Georgia bars recovery at 50% (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) and South Carolina above 50% (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Roden Law brings defective product claims on contingency and offers a free consultation at its offices in Georgia and South Carolina.

A maritime injury claim starts with which law governs, because work on vessels, docks and at the ports can fall outside the ordinary state rules. Where Georgia or South Carolina law applies, the filing deadline is two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). The answer depends on your duties, how much of your time is spent aboard a vessel, and where you were hurt, so record your employer, the vessel's name and the location immediately. In a state-law negligence suit, your fault bars recovery at 50% in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) or above 50% in South Carolina (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Roden Law handles maritime cases on contingency and consults free at its Georgia and South Carolina offices.

A spinal cord injury claim must be filed within two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530), even though the extent of paralysis may take months to establish. Case value rests on a life care plan: surgery, rehabilitation, attendant care, home and vehicle modifications, and lifetime lost earnings. When the injury happens at work in South Carolina, compensation benefits for paraplegia or quadriplegia continue for life (S.C. Code § 42-9-10). In a negligence suit, Georgia permits recovery below 50% fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), and South Carolina at no more than 50% (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Roden Law represents people with spinal cord injuries for a contingency fee, and the first meeting at its offices in both states is free.

The deadline to sue for a traumatic brain injury is two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530), so start before symptoms like memory loss have fully emerged. When a head injury comes from a crash, the states treat seat belts differently. Georgia admits evidence that you were unbelted, and it may reduce your recovery (O.C.G.A. § 40-8-76.1). South Carolina bars that evidence in civil cases (S.C. Code § 56-5-6540). You can still recover with partial fault: under 50% in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), and 50% or less in South Carolina (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Roden Law takes brain injury cases on contingency, with a free consultation at its Georgia and South Carolina offices.

A dog bite claim must be filed within two years in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and within three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Report the bite to animal control that day; the report records the dog, its owner and any earlier complaints. Payment usually comes from the owner's homeowner's or renter's insurance, and what a landlord knew about the dog is worth checking. Facial bites can leave scars that need years of treatment. In a negligence claim, a Georgia victim found 50% or more at fault cannot recover (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33); a South Carolina victim can recover at 50% or less (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Roden Law handles dog bite claims on contingency and provides a free consultation at its offices in Georgia and South Carolina.

If you were hurt at work, tell your employer quickly: Georgia requires notice within 30 days (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-80), and South Carolina within 90 days (S.C. Code § 42-15-20). In Georgia, the claim must be filed within one year from the date of injury, one year from the last remedial treatment your employer furnished, or two years from the last weekly benefit payment (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82). In South Carolina, it is due within two years of the accident (S.C. Code § 42-15-40). Workers' compensation is no-fault in both states, so ordinary carelessness does not reduce benefits; South Carolina denies them only for intoxication or a wilful intent to injure (S.C. Code § 42-9-60). Roden Law represents injured workers on contingency, with free consultations at its Georgia and South Carolina offices.

A Georgia wrongful death suit must be filed within two years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33). Its damages are measured by the full value of the life of the person who died (O.C.G.A. § 51-4-1). In South Carolina the deadline is generally three years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530), and only the estate's personal representative can bring the action (S.C. Code §§ 15-51-10, 15-51-20). A jury there may add punitive damages when the death resulted from recklessness, wilfulness or malice (S.C. Code § 15-51-40). The fault that matters is the deceased's: Georgia bars the claim at 50% or more (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), and South Carolina above 50% (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Roden Law represents grieving families on contingency, with a free consultation at offices in both states.

In Georgia, a medical malpractice claim must be filed within two years of the date the injury or death occurred, and generally no more than five years after the negligent act (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71). South Carolina allows three years from the treatment or from when the injury was or should have been discovered, but generally no more than six years (S.C. Code § 15-3-545). Before suing in South Carolina, you must file a Notice of Intent with a qualified expert's affidavit and mediate (S.C. Code §§ 15-79-125, 15-36-100); the notice tolls the deadline. Your fault bars recovery at 50% in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) and above 50% in South Carolina (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Roden Law takes malpractice cases on contingency and consults free at offices in both states.

Riders hurt by a negligent motorist have two years to file in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). South Carolina gives every motorcycle full use of its lane and prohibits riding between lanes of traffic (S.C. Code § 56-5-3640); its helmet requirement covers only riders under 21 (S.C. Code § 56-5-3660). Expect the insurer to say the rider caused the crash. A Georgia rider can still recover while less than 50% at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33), and a South Carolina rider while 50% or less at fault (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.), minus that percentage. Roden Law represents injured motorcyclists on a contingency fee, and consultations at its offices in both states are free.

After a fall in a store, restaurant or apartment complex, you have two years to file in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three years in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). Cameras overwrite footage and spills get mopped, so ask for the incident report and photograph the spot that day. Georgia defendants have two fault defenses. Apportionment bars recovery once you are 50% or more at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). A separate rule defeats the claim entirely if ordinary care would have let you avoid the consequences of the owner's negligence (O.C.G.A. § 51-11-7). South Carolina allows recovery if your fault is 50% or less (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Roden Law handles fall cases on contingency and consults free at its offices in Georgia and South Carolina.

A truck wreck claim usually targets a commercial carrier as well as its driver. Georgia defines a commercial motor vehicle as 10,001 pounds gross vehicle weight rating or more (O.C.G.A. § 40-1-1) and requires a commercial driver's license from 26,001 pounds (O.C.G.A. § 40-5-142), which bears on whether the driver needed one. The filing deadline is two years after the crash in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). If the carrier blames you, Georgia still allows recovery below 50% fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) and South Carolina up to 50% (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Roden Law handles truck cases on contingency, with no-cost consultations at its Georgia and South Carolina offices.

After a car crash, you have two years to sue in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and three in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-530). If the at-fault driver is uninsured, your own policy may pay: uninsured motorist coverage is mandatory on every South Carolina auto policy (S.C. Code § 38-77-150), and Georgia insurers must offer it (O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11). Insurers often argue both drivers share the blame. In Georgia that ends your claim only if you are 50% or more responsible (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33); in South Carolina, only if you are more than 50% responsible (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). Otherwise your award shrinks by your percentage. Roden Law's car accident lawyers work for a contingency fee and offer a free consultation at offices across Georgia and South Carolina.
